T1.reason: New constructions have meaning and conditions before dependent use: width/height, staircase volume, common sample-choice limit, moving endpoint, per-loan age and simple-interest premise.

locator.value: R1 — notes introduction and section 1 through Q1. Starting premises are the baseline's rectangle area, coordinates, function evaluation, sigma notation and monotone rectangle bounds. The lesson identifies fixed b and varying n, places interval i between (i−1)b/n and ib/n, selects right height (ib/n)² and multiplies by width. The resulting factor b³/n³ and Σi² are checked by direct substitution b=1,n=4. Figure 1 maps each orange top to the right blue graph point. Left/right height comparison warrants L≤A≤R; cancellation of the same interior samples warrants R−L=(b/n)(b²−0). Q1 can be reached using just those constructions, with changed b and an explicitly requested bound interpretation. No x² antiderivative or later square-sum limit is needed at this early attempt.

T2.reason: Every consequential unfamiliar form is built and read: b³/n³Σi², scaled cross sections, general c_i sum, definite integral/dummy variable, A(b), growth-weighted integral and endpoint brackets.

locator.value: R4 — section 3 endpoints, arbitrary samples and Figure 3. Definitions x_i=a+iΔx and Δx=(b−a)/n precede sample c_i use. The sample belongs to [x_{i−1},x_i] and is not necessarily a midpoint or endpoint; the figure locates it off-centre and shows full width Δx. The sigma sum is expanded exactly. The x+2 midpoint example builds two intervals, samples, heights and contributions and then reads those parts back from the expression. Exact midpoint area in this linear case follows from the average of each trapezium's endpoint heights, using baseline trapezium geometry; it is explicitly not generalized to all functions.

T3.reason: Pivotal transitions have warrants: geometry and similarity, positive division, squeeze gap, continuity strip bound, declared simple interest and dimensional conversion.

locator.value: R2 — section 2 construction, Figure 2 and bound. The move from two-dimensional area to three-dimensional sum representation is explained as an auxiliary volume, with each square footprint k² multiplied by unit thickness. A square-pyramid formula is explicitly introduced as a standard geometric premise rather than silently assumed from baseline (which lists a cone formula but not this pyramid formula). Common centre and parallel sides let side inequalities imply nested squares. The slab side n−j is fixed on layer j; similar triangles give n−z and n+1−z. j≤z≤j+1 then licenses both inequalities without a guessed visual conclusion. The numerical section n=4,z=1.5 checks which side belongs to which solid. Volume monotonicity and regions of positive excess give strict bounds. The original “prism” label is corrected, with the distinction explained.

T4.reason: Connected cases run width→sample→sum→limit; geometry→bound→area; moving-edge difference→derivative; per-loan principal→growth→total.

locator.value: R9 — section 5 interest weighting. The formula P(1+rτ) is introduced as the declared simple-interest model; τ is duration and rτ dimensionless. Calendar time t enters only after duration has a distinct role. A loan at t_i waits until 1, hence duration 1−t_i. The 9-month example checks 1/4-year growth; endpoint examples distinguish 1−t from t. Principal and multiplier are labelled underbraces before the product is summed and integrated. The whole integrand is explicitly interpreted as settlement debt per unit borrowing time. A full-year multiplier on all principal would be a different model. The general T form changes both the upper endpoint and the remaining duration together.

T5.reason: Applicable to all C1–C7 teaching capabilities. Early Q1 follows the first usable result; Q2 changes thickness, Q3 changes origin and monotonicity, Q4 lower boundary, Q5 borrowing timing, Q6 signed rate and total/average distinction.

locator.value: R10 — section 5 connected calculations and Q5. Constant borrowing is integrated to principal 12000 and debt 12360; the half-year average age interpretation follows from integrating 1−t. Twelve month-end lump loans produce 12330 through a finite arithmetic sum, with later timing explaining the lower interest. Thus the learner has grounds to choose a continuous integral or a finite sum from the timing premise. Q5 supplies f(t)=24000t and the same model, and requires one-loan construction, total principal/debt, changed timing interpretation and units. Expanding the polynomial uses only already available algebra and power integration. No actual loan-product knowledge is needed.

T6.reason: All six generated tasks identify requested outputs and discriminating explanations; no retained task depends on undisclosed incidental facts. Q3 and Q6 require actual choices rather than headings giving a method.

locator.value: R11 — ending Q6. The suggested later return is adjustable, no claimed universal schedule. The velocity premise is fully supplied; the baseline grants velocity/displacement/distance meanings. Earlier signed/magnitude accumulation and mean value tell the learner to locate the zero t=2, subtract below-axis area for net displacement and add magnitude for distance, then divide by 3 seconds. The representation recall component separately requires width 3/n and right sample 3i/n. This is a meaningful signed-rate application rather than numerical repetition of Q5.
